name: Grip and forearm training

image.caption: US Army 53442 BAGHDAD-San Benito, Tex. native, 1st Lt. Mike Olvera (left), uses his forearm to block Plant City Fla. native, Spc. David Croft's simulated knife attack during combined combatives training with their

lead: Grip and forearm training exercises the muscles that close the hand and move the wrist, with wrist curls, dead hangs, loaded carries and grippers. In looksmaxxing and physique circles it is used for bigger forearms, which posters describe as part of a strong, masculine arm and wrist look.

The forearm has a front (flexor) group that flexes the wrist and fingers, a back (extensor) group, muscles that rotate the forearm, and the brachioradialis, an elbow flexor. Training loads these muscles so they adapt as other muscles do under resistance. Published studies, mostly in athletes or lab settings, include a 4-week unilateral forearm trial that increased endurance time, 12-week programs in high school baseball players and a hybrid method that reported gains in forearm strength and mass in healthy men. No study examines perceived attractiveness, and wrist circumference and bone structure are described as unchanged by training.

paras: Lifters add a few forearm and grip exercises at the end of arm or back workouts, or build grip through hangs and carries. Strength sports also treat grip as a performance factor in pulling lifts. Size gains build over weeks to months.
Forearm training is generally low-risk exercise. Overuse of the wrist and elbow tendons is a general concern with repetitive loading.

angle.text: Lifters use wrist curls, hangs, carries and grippers to build forearm size and grip strength, valued for thicker, more muscular-looking arms. Loading the forearm muscles makes them adapt like other muscles. Published trials mostly measure strength, endurance or size, not how attractive the result looks.

lead: Grip and forearm training refers to exercise aimed at the muscles of the forearm and hand, which produce wrist movement and gripping force. Practitioners use movements such as wrist curls, dead hangs, loaded carries and gripper devices, and in strength sports grip is also treated as a performance factor in pulling lifts.

In looksmaxxing communities the topic is raised mainly for appearance: thick forearms are described by posters as part of a strong, masculine arm and wrist look. Related discussion concerns wrist circumference and bone structure, which proponents say training cannot change.

Published research on forearm training is sparse and mostly concerns function rather than looks. Studies include a 4-week unilateral forearm training trial that increased endurance time during rhythmic handgrip [1], 12-week wrist and forearm programs in high school baseball players [2][3], and a hybrid training method that reported increases in forearm strength and mass in healthy men [4]. No study found examines perceived attractiveness.
infobox: Wrist and finger flexors and extensors, brachioradialis, pronators and supinators
Dumbbells, barbells, pull-up bars, hand grippers

paras: The forearm is divided into an anterior compartment holding most of the wrist and finger flexors and a posterior compartment holding the extensors. The anterior muscles include flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor carpi ulnaris, pronator teres and the finger flexors; the posterior group includes extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, extensor digitorum, extensor carpi ulnaris and supinator, with the brachioradialis sitting in the posterior compartment but acting as an elbow flexor [5]. Anatomy references note that the flexors are bulkier than the extensors [5].

Forum posters who discuss forearms describe a mix of direct isolation work (wrist flexion and extension), hanging and carrying movements, and the indirect load that pulling exercises such as pull-ups and rows place on the grip. Some beginner calisthenics and home-workout threads treat grip as a by-product of bar work rather than a separate focus. This article does not describe specific protocols.

Grip strength is conventionally measured with a hand dynamometer such as the Jamar type, and the results are compared against normative data. Clinical use of such testing is described mainly in the context of hand pathology, nerve and tendon injury and rehabilitation [6].
No studies found testing forearm or grip training for appearance, such as perceived attractiveness or arm aesthetics. The following related research examines function and muscle adaptations.

A study of unilateral non-dominant forearm training over 4 weeks reported that endurance time rose by 102% in the trained arm during rhythmic handgrip, with effects on the blood-pressure response to exercise [1]. A related earlier study found that forearm training attenuated sympathetic responses to prolonged rhythmic forearm exercise [7]. A 12-week wrist and forearm program in high school baseball players was evaluated for sport performance [2][3], and a hybrid training method was reported to increase forearm muscle strength and mass in healthy men without harming hand function [4]. The abstracts available focus on physiology and function, not on visual outcome.

lore.intro: Forearm and grip work is discussed on looksmax.org mainly inside general calisthenics and home-workout threads, where grip is treated as a part of arm development.

claims.claim: Pulling and hanging exercises build the forearms without direct wrist work.
Dedicated forearm training makes the forearms bigger and stronger.
Thicker forearms make a person look more masculine or attractive.
